fields.label: Definition & Explanation
fields.value: Reopening of theatres in 1660 (King's Company under Thomas Killigrew; Duke's Company under William Davenant) introduced indoor proscenium stages and professional actresses (Margaret Hughes, Nell Gwyn). Comedy of Manners peaked in Etherege's The Man of Mode, Wycherley's The Country Wife, and Congreve's The Way of the World (1700), attacked by Jeremy Collier's A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698). In the 18th century, John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728) invented Ballad Opera, and Goldsmith (She Stoops to Conquer, 1773) and Sheridan (The Rivals 1775, The School for Scandal 1777) revived laughing comedy against sentimental comedy.

fields.value: Romantic Personal Essay: Charles Lamb ('Elia' — 'Dream-Children: A Reverie', 'A Dissertation upon Roast Pig'), William Hazlitt (Table-Talk, The Spirit of the Age, 'On Going a Journey'), Thomas De Quincey (Confessions of an English Opium-Eater 1821, 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth', 'The Literature of Knowledge and the Literature of Power'). Victorian Sages: Thomas Carlyle (Sartor Resartus, Past and Present, On Heroes and Hero-Worship), John Ruskin (Modern Painters, The Seven Lamps of Architecture, The Stones of Venice ['The Nature of Gothic'], Unto This Last, Sesame and Lilies), John Stuart Mill (On Liberty 1859, The Subjection of Women 1869), Cardinal Newman (The Idea of a University, Apologia Pro Vita Sua), Matthew Arnold (Culture and Anarchy 1869), Walter Pater (Studies in the History of the Renaissance 1873). Modern Prose: Lytton Strachey (Eminent Victorians 1918: Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Dr. Arnold, General Gordon), Virginia Woolf (A Room of One's Own 1929, Three Guineas 1938), George Orwell ('Shooting an Elephant', 'Marrakech', 'Politics and the English Language').

fields.label: Exam Cue / Trap
fields.value: De Quincey coined the distinction between 'Literature of Knowledge' (teaches) and 'Literature of Power' (moves) in his 1848 essay on Pope.
